name: Esther Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Esther. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Your name won't go on anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the surgery on Market Street in a small farming town, about four thousand people plus the farms around it. A lot of my patients are older, so it's blood pressure, chests, hips, sugar, and quite a bit of sitting with people after bad news. On Thursdays I do home visits out to the farms, which is the part I like best.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing families. I've only been here three years and I already know which farmer won't come in unless his wife books it for him. What wears me out is the computer: every click, every box, every form the health board invents. The practice manager keeps asking me to try the AI note-taker, and I keep saying no thank you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Daniel two summers ago; he sells tractors and farm machinery at the dealership on the bypass. We rent a cottage from my uncle at a fair price and we've got about three months of costs put by. We'd like to start a family in the next year or two, God willing, and buy a house before then if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd expect, frankly. A lot of noise and then life carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, politely. At the practice meeting I'd say we can stop being pushed to use the note-taker, since it's not changing anything. I don't go online much, but at church I'd say the same to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I trained to sit across from a person and listen, not to check what a machine wrote about them. Nobody else at the practice wants to do the Thursday farm visits, so my job here is secure whatever the computers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Write my own notes, see my patients, do my visits. Daniel and I would keep putting money by for a house deposit, about 500 a month between us, and I'd keep refusing the note-taker however nicely the manager asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. The kind of feeling you get when the weather forecast turns out wrong and it's a nice day after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the practice manager. How hard does she push?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's polite about it. Every month or so there's an email about how many minutes the other doctors save. I'd rather stay late than have a program listening to my patients, and I've told her that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about money or work that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the house. Prices round here have gone up since city people started buying weekend cottages. If Daniel's dealership has a bad year, that slows us down too, but that's farming towns for you; it's not AI.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, politely, at the practice meeting.
We can **stop being pushed** to use the AI note-taker.
think: I'd be **relieved**; I trained to listen, not to check a machine's notes.
The town **needs doctors**, so my job here is secure.
do: Keep **writing her own notes** and doing the Thursday farm visits.
Save about **500 a month** with Daniel towards a house deposit.
Keep **refusing the note-taker** however nicely she's asked.
feel: **Calm** and settled, like a bad forecast turning into a nice day.
S0.quote: Nobody else at the practice wants to do the Thursday farm visits, so my job here is secure whatever the computers do.
fieldNote: Her **refusal** of the note-taker is a matter of principle, not just habit.
She draws security from **rural need**: nobody else wants the farm visits.
Her real money pressure is **house prices**, pushed up by weekend buyers.

steps.text: Keep writing her own notes and doing Thursday farm visits
Save 500 a month with Daniel towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the health board's dream, honestly. Fewer staff, more screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I believe: medicine isn't a booking system, and patients deserve a doctor who actually reads their letters. I'd say it at the practice meeting and to the local doctors' association. I'd be polite, but I wouldn't pretend to be pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried for myself. If every other doctor at our surgery uses the AI to see four more patients a day and I don't, I look slow. And when the partners decide who gets fewer sessions, they'll look at the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my way, but I'd stay later to keep my numbers up, maybe until seven most nights. I'd join the doctors' association group that's pushing for a human doctor to sign off every result. And we'd skip the summer holiday this year and save it, because I'd want a bigger cushion if my sessions get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. And a bit stubborn about it, which I know doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay late rather than use the tool. What would Daniel say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm being pig-headed, and he'd be partly right. He uses software at the dealership for every quote. But he also knows I'd rather be tired than hand my patients over to a program I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if this happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies selling it, and the health ministry for buying whatever's cheapest. Nobody asked the old man with chest pain whether he wanted to explain it to a screen. He'd just stop coming in, and we'd find out too late.

say: **Medicine isn't** a booking system; patients deserve a doctor who reads their letters.
I'd say it to the **doctors' association**, politely but not pleased.
think: If colleagues see **four more patients** a day with AI, I look slow.
The **slow doctor** is the one who loses sessions.
do: Stay until **seven most nights** to keep her patient numbers up.
Join the **association group** pushing for human sign-off on every result.
Skip **this year's holiday** to build a bigger cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, and **stubborn** about it, which she admits doesn't help.
S1.quote: If every other doctor at our surgery uses the AI to see four more patients a day and I don't, I look slow.
fieldNote: She sees the risk to her sessions clearly but **digs in** rather than adapt.
She blames **tech firms** and **the ministry** for buying whatever's cheapest.
Her husband calls her **pig-headed**, and she half agrees.

steps.text: Stay at the surgery until seven to keep her numbers up
Join the doctors' association group demanding human sign-off on results

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Two years? That's frightening. That's not enough time for anybody to do anything sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say it's dangerous and should be slowed down, that no machine should make medical decisions without a doctor answering for them. I'd say it at church, at the practice, and to our local representative if I got the chance. I'd say it quite loudly, for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose most of my work. I'm the doctor who won't use it, in a practice that would have to use it to survive. The farm visits might keep me going until the robots come in 2031, but a practice can't pay a full-time doctor for one day of visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could: the car upgrade, eating out, the house hunt. We'd put off trying for a baby, which is the hardest thing to say out loud. And I'd lean on family: my uncle's cottage is cheap, and Daniel's parents have a farm where we could live if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. I'd pray about it, honestly, and I'd still be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still refuse the AI. Even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to learn it to keep any job at all, and I'd hate every minute. But by 2028 the AI wouldn't need a doctor to drive it anyway, so learning it wouldn't save me. That's what makes it so bleak: there's no right move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for work, if medicine shrank that much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. That's the honest answer. Maybe the hands-on side, caring for the elderly out on the farms, until 2031. I've no plan beyond that, and I don't like having no plan.

say: It's **dangerous**; no machine should decide on care without a doctor **answering for it**.
I'd say it at church, at work and to our **local representative**.
think: I'd **lose most** of my work as the doctor who won't use AI.
**Farm visits** alone can't pay a full-time doctor, even until 2031.
do: Cut the **car upgrade**, eating out and the house hunt.
Put off **trying for a baby** until the picture is clearer.
Fall back on **family**: the cheap cottage and Daniel's parents' farm.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake even after praying about it.
**Trapped**, since learning AI wouldn't save her job either.
S2.quote: We'd put off trying for a baby, which is the hardest thing to say out loud.
fieldNote: She sees **no right move**: refusing AI and learning it both lose.
Delaying **a baby** is the cost she finds hardest to name.
Her fallback is **family and land**, not government help, which fits her views.

steps.text: Cancel the car upgrade and stop eating out
Put off trying for a baby with Daniel
Lean on her uncle's cheap cottage and Daniel's parents' farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two. Still too fast for my liking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that a doctor must answer for every decision, but I'd say it more calmly. With five years there's time for rules, and I'd want the doctors' association to get them written before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be in trouble eventually, but not straight away. Daniel's job worries me too. Selling tractors is mostly quoting, ordering and talking, so my husband's job could be squeezed around the same time as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for now, my own notes, my own patients. We'd save harder, aiming for six months put by instead of three. And I'd write to our local representative asking for a law that a real doctor signs off every diagnosis, because if that's the rule, there's still a job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sharp than the two-year one, but it sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the baby, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead, I think, maybe next year. Five years is long enough that I'd rather not spend it waiting. My grandmother was a midwife through hard times, and people still had children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on as you are. Would you learn the AI tools at any point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the practice made it a rule, yes, grudgingly. I'm not going to resign over a note-taker. But I wouldn't go looking for it, and I'd be the last one at Market Street to switch.

say: A doctor must **answer for every decision**, and I'd say it calmly.
With five years, the association should **get rules written** before 2031.
think: I'd be in trouble **eventually**, but not straight away.
Selling tractors is mostly quoting, so **Daniel's job** could be squeezed too.
do: Carry on with **her own notes** and patients for now.
Save towards **six months** of costs instead of three.
Write to the **local representative** asking for doctor sign-off by law.
feel: **Anxious**, less sharp than the two-year picture, but **always there**.
S3.quote: Selling tractors is mostly quoting, ordering and talking, so my husband's job could be squeezed around the same time as mine.
fieldNote: She notices **both incomes** in her household are exposed at once.
Her hope rests on a **legal rule** requiring a doctor's sign-off.
She'd learn AI only if **made to**, and would switch last.

steps.text: Keep writing her own notes at the Market Street surgery
Build savings with Daniel up to six months of costs
Write to the local representative asking for doctor sign-off by law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, with children by then, I hope. That feels further away than the date sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, with doctors in charge, and that we shouldn't let the companies rush us. I'd probably say it less often, to be honest, because ten years feels like someone else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think people out here will still want a real doctor for a long time, even if the city goes all in. The old farmers I visit on Thursdays wouldn't let a robot into their kitchens, but I know that's partly me hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different in the first year. Keep my patients, keep my notes, start a family with Daniel and save for a house. If the AI is still coming in five years, I'd look again then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a far-off way. Like knowing the river floods every few years: you don't move house over it, but you keep sandbags in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look again in five years. What would you be looking for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether patients are actually choosing it. If the young families in town start booking the AI instead of me, that's when I'd worry properly. Until then, I'm not changing how I practise on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and with people. My grandmother's midwifery, my uncle's farm, Daniel's trade. I'd want them to have a skill the town can't do without, whatever the computers are doing.

say: There's time to do this properly, with **doctors in charge**.
I'd say it **less often**, since ten years feels like someone else's problem.
think: Older **farm patients** will want a real doctor for a long time.
I know that's **partly hoping**, not knowing.
do: Keep her **patients and notes** as they are in the first year.
Start a **family** with Daniel and keep saving for a house.
**Look again** in five years at whether patients choose AI.
feel: **Uneasy** in a far-off way, like keeping **sandbags** in the shed.
S4.quote: The old farmers I visit on Thursdays wouldn't let a robot into their kitchens, but I know that's partly me hoping.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **set the worry** aside almost entirely.
Her test is **patient choice**: young families booking AI over her.
She wants her children to have **hands-on skills** the town needs.

steps.text: Keep her patients and her own notes at Market Street
Check in five years whether young families are booking AI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years, with both Daniel and me squeezed and a baby put off. What would help is a clear rule that a doctor answers for every diagnosis, and family nearby, which thank God we have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about trust. People out here tell their doctor things they wouldn't tell their own family, because they've known the surgery for forty years. You can't download forty years.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked the old man with chest pain whether he wanted to explain it to a screen.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old GP** in a small farming town, married to Daniel, who sells tractors.
She **refuses AI tools** on principle and would rather stay late than use a note-taker.
Her sense of security rests on **rural need** and the Thursday farm visits nobody else wants.
In the fast scenarios she'd **delay a baby** and lean on family land.
She blames **tech firms** and a cost-cutting ministry, and hopes a law keeps doctors signing off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which squeezes both incomes and delays a baby.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **legal rule** that a doctor answers for every diagnosis.
